'''Composite measure''' in statistics and research design refer to composite measures of [[Variable and attribute (research)|variable]]s, i.e. measurements based on multiple data items.<ref name="Babbie2012-162">{{cite book|author=Earl Babbie|title=The Practice of Social Research|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=k-aza3qSULoC&pg=PA162|date=1 January 2012|publisher=Cengage Learning|isbn=1-133-04979-6|page=162}}</ref>

An example of a composite measure is an [[IQ test]], which gives a single score based on a series of responses to various questions.

Three common composite measures include:
* [[Index (statistics)|indexes]] - measures that summarize and rank specific observations, usually on the [[ordinal scale]];<ref name="Babbie2012-162"/>
* [[Scale (social sciences)|scales]] - advanced indexes whose observations are further transformed (scaled) due to their logical or empirical relationships;<ref name="Babbie2012-162"/>
* [[Typology (statistics)|typologies]] - measures that classify observations in terms of their attributes on multiple variables, usually on a [[nominal scale]].<ref name="Babbie2012-162"/>

==Indexes versus scales==
Indexes are often referred to as scales, but in fact not all indexes are scales.<ref name="Babbie2012-164">{{cite book|author=Earl Babbie|title=The Practice of Social Research|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=k-aza3qSULoC&pg=PA164|date=1 January 2012|publisher=Cengage Learning|isbn=1-133-04979-6|page=164}}</ref>

Whereas indexes are usually created by aggregating scores assigned to individual [[Variable and attribute (research)|attributes]] of various variables, scales are more nuanced and take into account differences in intensity among the attribute of the same variable in question.<ref name="Babbie2012-162"/> Indexes and scales should provide an [[ordinal scale|ordinal ranking]] of cases on a given variable, though scales are usually more efficient at this.<ref name="Babbie2012-177">{{cite book|author=Earl Babbie|title=The Practice of Social Research|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=k-aza3qSULoC&pg=PA164|date=1 January 2012|publisher=Cengage Learning|isbn=1-133-04979-6|page=177}}</ref><ref name="Babbie2012-185">{{cite book|author=Earl Babbie|title=The Practice of Social Research|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=k-aza3qSULoC&pg=PA185|date=1 January 2012|publisher=Cengage Learning|isbn=1-133-04979-6|page=185}}</ref> While indexes are based on a simple aggregation of [[indicator (social sciences)|indicators]] of a variable, scales are more advanced, and their calculations may be more complex, using for example scaling procedures such as [[semantic differential]].<ref name="Babbie2012-185"/>

==Composite measure validation==
A good composite measure will ensure that the indicators are independent of one another.<ref name="Babbie2012-173-175">{{cite book|author=Earl Babbie|title=The Practice of Social Research|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=k-aza3qSULoC&pg=PA173|date=1 January 2012|publisher=Cengage Learning|isbn=1-133-04979-6|pages=173-175}}</ref> It should also successfully predict other indicators of the variable.<ref name="Babbie2012-173-175"/>
